etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English widren, wydderen (“to dry up, shrivel”), related to or perhaps an alteration of Middle English wederen (“to expose to weather”), from Old English wederian (“to expose to weather, exhibit a change of weather”).

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To shrivel, droop or dry up, especially from lack of water.
(transitive) To cause to shrivel or dry up.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Matthew 12:10:
quote.text: There was a man which had his hand withered.

quote.citation: c. 1590–1592 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Taming of the Shrew”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act IV, scene v]:
quote.text: This is man, old, wrinkled, faded, withered.

quote.citation: 1700, [John] Dryden, “Palamon and Arcite: Or, The Knight’s Tale. In Three Books.”, in Fables Ancient and Modern; […], London:  […]  Jacob Tonson, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: now warm in love, now with'ring in the grave

definitions.definition: (intransitive, figurative) To lose vigour or power; to languish; to pass away.

quote.citation: 1812–1818, Lord Byron, “(please specify |canto=I to IV)”, in Childe Harold’s Pilgrimage. , London: John Murray,, (please specify the stanza number):

quote.text: States thrive or wither as moons wax and wane.

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To become helpless due to emotion.
(transitive) To make helpless due to emotion.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: See the etymology of the corresponding lemma form.

definitions.definition: singular of withers (“part of the back of a four-legged animal that is between the shoulder blades”)

quote.text: Timozel had slid his feet quickly from the stirrups and swung his leg over the horse's wither as it slumped to the ground, standing himself in one graceful movement.

quote.citation: 2008, Kate Luxmoore, Introduction to Equestrian Sports, →ISBN, page 140:
quote.text: If a saddle tips too far forward it may rest on the horse's wither and cause pain. There should always be a gap of roughly 5 cm between the horse's wither and the pommel when you are sitting on the saddle.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English wither, from Old English wiþer (“again, against”, adverb in compounds), from Proto-West Germanic *wiþr (“against, toward”).

definitions.definition: (obsolete or chiefly in compounds) Against, in opposition to.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English witheren, from Old English wiþerian (“to resist, oppose, struggle against”).
